specAnchors.text: describe the evolution of stars of similar mass to the Sun through the following stages: • nebula • star (main sequence) • red giant • white dwarf

primer.text: Every Sun-sized star repeats the same biography: it condenses from a nebula into a protostar, ignites fusion as a main sequence star, swells into a red giant when the hydrogen runs low, and ends as a fading white dwarf. Learn the four stages in order and the physics at each turn.

modules.title: From nebula to protostar
sourceHeadings: Summary of the life cycles of stars
modules.opening: All stars begin inside a nebula — an enormous drifting cloud of gas and dust. Gravity draws the particles inward until a hot ball of gas forms — the protostar — whose density rises, collisions become more frequent, and temperature climbs.
keyPoints: Stars are born inside nebulae — enormous clouds of gas and dust drifting between the stars.
Gravity within the nebula pulls particles closer together.
The collapsing cloud becomes a hot ball of gas: a protostar.
As the protostar's density rises, more frequent collisions push its temperature up.

low.restatement: Nebula collapses under gravity → hot dense protostar → fusion ignites.
low.analogy: A snowball rolling downhill gathers itself tighter and warms from the squeezing — then finally 'lights up'.
low.examPointer: Sequence questions want the arrow order; the nebula always comes first.

medium.restatement: Collapse concentrates particles, so collision frequency — and therefore temperature — climbs until fusion can start.
medium.analogy: Pumping a bicycle pump: compressing the air inside warms it.
medium.examPointer: Tie density up → collisions up → temperature up in one sentence for the explanation mark.

modules.title: Main sequence and red giant
modules.opening: Once fusion ignites, the star joins the main sequence and holds itself in stable equilibrium. After several billion years the hydrogen begins to run out, core fusion dies down, and the star fuses helium instead — swelling outward and cooling into a red giant.
keyPoints: A star that initiates fusion is a main sequence star, in stable equilibrium.
Several billion years in, the hydrogen begins to run low.
The core fusion reactions die down, and the star begins fusing helium.
Helium fusion makes the outer star expand; the cooling surface turns it into a red giant.

low.restatement: Fusion ignites → stable main sequence → hydrogen fades → helium fusion swells the star into a red giant.
low.analogy: A log fire: steady burn (main sequence), then the logs collapse and the flames spread wide but cooler (red giant).
low.examPointer: Six-mark lifecycle answers score on order — always name the fuel that changes at each turn.

medium.restatement: The red giant turn is a fuel story: hydrogen exhaustion switches the core to helium, and the swelling surface cools and reddens.
medium.analogy: A balloon inflating as the air inside is rearranged — bigger outside, cooler at the skin.
medium.examPointer: 'Red giant' then 'white dwarf' — never insert a supernova for a Sun-mass star.

modules.title: The white dwarf ending
modules.opening: When the helium fusion reactions finish, the star collapses into a white dwarf. The white dwarf cools over time, so the energy it emits decreases, until the faded remnant gives out no light at all — the black dwarf stage.
keyPoints: Once helium fusion finishes, the star collapses into a white dwarf.
White dwarfs cool steadily as the ages pass.
As it cools, the energy a white dwarf emits decreases.
A fully faded white dwarf that no longer emits light is a black dwarf.

low.restatement: Fusion ends → collapse → white dwarf, which cools and fades toward black.
low.analogy: A charcoal briquette after the fire: still glowing (white dwarf), then greyer and darker as the night wears on (black dwarf).
low.examPointer: White dwarf cools and dims — keep 'black dwarf' only for the no-light endpoint.

medium.restatement: The endpoint is radiative retirement: no fuel, no fusion, just cooling and dimming.
medium.analogy: An unplanned power cut in a city: the lights fade as the stored energy drains.
medium.examPointer: Emission decreases as temperature decreases — write both clauses.

glossary.definition: An enormous cloud of gas and dust drifting between the stars, where stars are born.
The hot, dense ball of gas formed as gravity collapses a nebula.
A star in stable equilibrium once fusion has begun in its core.
The collapsed, cooling endpoint of a solar-mass star.

figures.alt: Flowchart showing star life cycle: gas cloud becomes protostar, then main sequence star. The paths then split, demonstrating that a star about the same size as the Sun will become a red giant,  white dwarf, and black dwarf. A star much bigger than the Sun will become a red supergiant, supernova, and either a neutron star or a black hole.
